claim: The evolution of metazoans from their unicellular ancestors was one of the most important events in the history of life.
source: The evolution of metazoans from their unicellular ancestors was one of the most important events in the history of life.
evidence: This is a statement of scientific consensus about the significance of metazoan evolution.

claim: Capsaspora owczarzaki exhibits an aggregative multicellular stage.
source: In this study, we describe an aggregative multicellular stage in the protist Capsaspora owczarzaki, a close unicellular relative of metazoans.
evidence: The manuscript presents observational and experimental data demonstrating aggregative behavior in C. owczarzaki.

claim: Capsaspora owczarzaki is a close unicellular relative of metazoans.
source: In this study, we describe an aggregative multicellular stage in the protist Capsaspora owczarzaki, a close unicellular relative of metazoans.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic relationships established in the literature.

claim: Transition to the aggregative stage in C. owczarzaki is associated with significant upregulation of orthologs of genes known to establish multicellularity and tissue architecture in metazoans.
source: Remarkably, transition to the aggregative stage is associated with significant upregulation of orthologs of genes known to establish multicellularity and tissue architecture in metazoans.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data showing differential gene expression patterns.

claim: C. owczarzaki exhibits transitions in regulated alternative splicing during its life cycle.
source: We further observe transitions in regulated alternative splicing during the C. owczarzaki life cycle, including the deployment of an exon network associated with signaling, a feature of splicing regulation so far only observed in metazoans.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of alternative splicing patterns across life cycle stages.

claim: C. owczarzaki deploys an exon network associated with signaling, a feature of splicing regulation so far only observed in metazoans.
source: We further observe transitions in regulated alternative splicing during the C. owczarzaki life cycle, including the deployment of an exon network associated with signaling, a feature of splicing regulation so far only observed in metazoans.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of differentially spliced exons enriched in protein kinase genes.

claim: Features of aggregative behavior in an ancestral protist may have been co-opted to develop some multicellular properties currently seen in metazoans.
source: Our results reveal the existence of a highly regulated aggregative stage in C. owczarzaki and further suggest that features of aggregative behavior in an ancestral protist may had been co-opted to develop some multicellular properties currently seen in metazoans.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed data and evolutionary relationships.

claim: The genetic repertoire of the metazoan unicellular ancestor was much more complex than previously thought.
source: In this regard, the analyses of unicellular holozoan genomes, that is choanoflagellates and filastereans, have shown that the genetic repertoire of the metazoan unicellular ancestor was much more complex than previously thought (Abedin and King, 2008; King et al., 2008; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2010; Suga et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genomic studies.

claim: Multicellularity has been independently acquired multiple times during the evolution of eukaryotes, in more than 20 different lineages.
source: Multicellularity has been independently acquired multiple times during the evolution of eukaryotes, in more than 20 different lineages including animals, plants, fungi, slime molds, green and brown algae, and several other eukaryotes (King, 2004; Parfrey and Lahr, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous evolutionary studies.

claim: Multicellular organisms evolved through two major strategies: aggregation of different cells or clonal division of a single cell.
source: Multicellular organisms evolved through two major strategies: aggregation of different cells or clonal division of a single cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge in evolutionary biology.

claim: The most complex multicellular organisms likely arose through clonal development rather than by aggregation of genetically diverse cells.
source: Multi-level selection theory has proposed that the most complex multicellular organisms likely arose through clonal development rather than by aggregation of genetically diverse cells, since intra-organismal competition in the latter might be expected to be evolutionarily unstable (Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007; Michod, 2007; Newman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on multi-level selection.

claim: Eukaryotic lineages that attained the most complex multicellular lifestyles (i.e., plants and metazoans) arose through clonal cell division.
source: Accordingly, eukaryotic lineages that attained the most complex multicellular lifestyles (i.e., plants and metazoans) arose through clonal cell division (Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to evolutionary literature.

claim: Aggregative cell behavior typically represents a transient life cycle stage.
source: In contrast to clonal multicellularity, aggregative cell behavior typically represents a transient life cycle stage.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of aggregative multicellularity in various organisms.

claim: Aggregative multicellularity arose within several eukaryotic clades, including the dictyostelids (Amoebozoa).
source: This type of multicellularity arose within several eukaryotic clades, including the dictyostelids (Amoebozoa) (Schaap, 2011), acrasid amoebas (Heterolobosea, Discicristata, Discoba) (Brown et al., 2011), Guttulinopsis vulgaris (Cercozoa, Rhizaria) (Brown et al., 2012), the genus Sorogena (Ciliata, Alveolata) (Lasek-Nesselquist and Katz, 2001), the holomycota Fonticula alba (Opisthokonta) (Brown et al., 2009) and the genus Sorodiplophrys (Labyrinthulomycetes, Heterokonta) (Dykstra and Olive, 1975)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of various aggregative organisms.

claim: Within the opisthokont clade, only Fonticula alba has been described to have aggregative behavior.
source: Within the opisthokont clade that comprises Metazoa, Fungi and their unicellular relatives (Cavalier-Smith, 2003; Steenkamp et al., 2006; Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008), so far only a single taxon has been described to have aggregative behavior, which is F. alba (Brown et al., 2009), a close relative of Fungi.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on F. alba and phylogenetic studies.

claim: Among close unicellular relatives of Metazoa, clonal development is the only known multicellular behavior, as described in choanoflagellates and ichthyosporeans.
source: Moreover, among close unicellular relatives of Metazoa, clonal development is the only known multicellular behavior, as described in choanoflagellates and ichthyosporeans (Dayel et al., 2011; Suga and Ruiz-Trillo, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of choanoflagellates and ichthyosporeans.

claim: Some metazoan cells show aggregative behaviors, including mesenchymal and germ line cells during development.
source: Within metazoans, which have largely clonal development, some cells show aggregative behaviors; for example, mesenchymal (O'Shea, 1987) and germ line cells (Savage and Danilchik, 1993) during development, sponge cells after cell dissociation (Wilson, 1907) and arthropod blood cells through active amoeboid movement (Loeb, 1903, 1921).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of cell behavior in metazoans.

claim: Capsaspora owczarzaki was isolated as an endosymbiont of the fresh-water snail Biomphalaria glabrata.
source: Isolated decades ago as an endosymbiont of the fresh-water snail Biomphalaria glabrata (Owczarzak et al., 1980), C. owczarzaki belongs to the clade Filasterea, the sister-group of Metazoa and choanoflagellates (Torruella et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original isolation study.

claim: C. owczarzaki belongs to the clade Filasterea, the sister-group of Metazoa and choanoflagellates.
source: Isolated decades ago as an endosymbiont of the fresh-water snail Biomphalaria glabrata (Owczarzak et al., 1980), C. owczarzaki belongs to the clade Filasterea, the sister-group of Metazoa and choanoflagellates (Torruella et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to phylogenetic studies.

claim: Filasterea also includes a free-living marine unicellular species known as Ministeria vibrans.
source: Filasterea also includes a free-living marine unicellular species known as Ministeria vibrans (Shalchian-Tabrizi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to taxonomic studies.

claim: C. owczarzaki differentiates into an amoeba that crawls over substrate.
source: Under initial culture conditions ('Materials and methods'), C. owczarzaki differentiates into an amoeba that crawls over substrate (Video 1), surveying its environment with its filopodia (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by video documentation and previous observations.

claim: At the filopodial stage, active DNA replication occurs with >10% of the cells in S-phase.
source: At this stage, active DNA replication occurs (with >10% of the cells in S-phase) and, within 48 hr, the cells enter an exponential growth phase (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Within 48 hr of the filopodial stage, C. owczarzaki cells enter an exponential growth phase.
source: At this stage, active DNA replication occurs (with >10% of the cells in S-phase) and, within 48 hr, the cells enter an exponential growth phase (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 2.

claim: After the filopodial stage, C. owczarzaki cells start to detach from the surface and begin to retract their filopodia and encyst.
source: Subsequently, the cells start to detach from the surface and begin to retract their filopodia and encyst (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 3.

claim: After 8 days, no attached amoebas remain and growth is stabilized.
source: After 8 days, no attached amoebas remain and growth is stabilized (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting and microscopy data.

claim: The cystic stage may represent a dispersal resistance form.
source: This cystic stage may represent a dispersal resistance form.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed cystic stage.

claim: C. owczarzaki cells actively form cell aggregates through an alternative developmental path.
source: Strikingly, we observe an alternative path to this process involving the active formation of cell aggregates (Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by video documentation of aggregate formation.

claim: In C. owczarzaki aggregates, cells attach to each other and produce cohesive extracellular material.
source: In these aggregates, the cells attach to each other and produce cohesive extracellular material (Figure 3D) until a compact cell aggregate, in which cells no longer bear filopodia, is formed (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 3.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy demonstrates the presence of a thick, unstructured, extracellular material within C. owczarzaki aggregates that appears to prevent direct contact between cells.
source: Transmission electron microscopy demonstrates the presence of a thick, unstructured, extracellular material within the aggregates that appears to prevent direct contact between cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by TEM images in Figure 3F.

claim: Clusters of C. owczarzaki cells appear to occur at random under normal culture conditions.
source: Clusters of cells appear to occur at random under normal culture conditions.
evidence: This is based on observations during normal culture.

claim: C. owczarzaki cell clusters are formed through aggregation of multiple cells, not by clonal division.
source: This indicates that cell clusters are not composed of daughter cells resulting from successive cell divisions, which would result in single-color cell clusters, but instead by aggregation of multiple cells.
evidence: This is supported by dual-staining experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: C. owczarzaki aggregates can form efficiently even when cell division is blocked by hydroxyurea and aphidicolin.
source: We also observed that aggregates could form efficiently even when cell division was blocked by two different inhibitors, hydroxyurea and aphidicolin (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experiments with cell division inhibitors shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The proliferation rate of aggregative C. owczarzaki cells is extremely low compared to filopodial cells.
source: Finally, by flow cytometry, we observed that the proliferation rate of aggregative cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) is extremely low (compared with the observations in Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: The observation of aggregative multicellularity in C. owczarzaki represents the first reported case in a close unicellular relative of Metazoa.
source: This observation represents the first reported case of aggregative multicellularity in a close unicellular relative of Metazoa.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and review of literature.

claim: Multiple cell types and behaviors (including aggregative behavior, flagellar motility, amoeboid movement, clonal colony formation) were most likely present among the unicellular ancestors of metazoans.
source: We can then infer that multiple cell types and behaviors (including aggregative behavior, flagellar motility, amoeboid movement, clonal colony formation, etc) were most likely present among the unicellular ancestors of metazoans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed diversity of behaviors in extant unicellular relatives.

claim: The range of cell behaviors in unicellular relatives may have provided the basis for the evolution of the diverse cell types seen in animals.
source: This range of cell behaviors may have provided the basis for the evolution of the diverse cell types seen in animals (Arendt, 2008; Arendt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to evolutionary theory.

claim: Each one of the three known unicellular lineages closely related to Metazoa (choanoflagellates, ichthyosporeans and filastereans) has some kind of simple multicellularity.
source: Interestingly, each one of the three known unicellular lineages closely related to Metazoa (choanoflagellates, ichthyosporeans and filastereans) has some kind of simple multicellularity.
evidence: This is based on observations from this study and previous literature.

claim: The tight regulation observed in C. owczarzaki emphasizes that a regulated temporal cell differentiation was already in place among unicellular ancestor of animals.
source: Moreover, the tight regulation observed in C. owczarzaki (see below) emphasizes that a regulated temporal cell differentiation was already in place among unicellular ancestor of animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed gene expression and splicing regulation data.

claim: During the transition to animal multicellularity, ancestral premetazoan cell types may have been integrated into a single multicellular entity by means of controlling cell differentiation spatially, rather than temporally.
source: This reinforces the view that, during the transition to animal multicellularity, ancestral premetazoan cell types may have been integrated into a single multicellular entity by means of controlling cell differentiation spatially, rather than temporally (Mikhailov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to evolutionary theory.

claim: Of 8637 annotated genes in C. owczarzaki, 4486 showed statistically significant differential regulation in one or more pair-wise comparisons between life cycle stages.
source: Of 8637 annotated genes, 4486 showed statistically significant differential regulation ('Materials and methods') in one or more pair-wise comparisons between life cycle stages, including 1354 changes between filopodial and aggregate stages, 3227 between filopodial and cystic stages, and 3096 between aggregate and cystic stages.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: Each C. owczarzaki cell stage has a specific transcriptomic profile.
source: Moreover, when performing one-versus-all comparisons, each cell stage had a specific transcriptomic profile (Figure 5A), indicating tight regulation at the level of gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Genes upregulated in the filopodial stage were enriched in signalling functions, such as tyrosine kinase activity and G-protein-coupled receptor activity.
source: Genes upregulated in the filopodial stage were enriched in signalling functions, such as tyrosine kinase activity and G-protein-coupled receptor activity, as well as in transcription factors, especially of the Basic Leucine Zipper Domain (bZIP) superfamily (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Genes involved in protein synthesis and DNA replication were significantly upregulated in the filopodial stage.
source: Genes involved in protein synthesis and DNA replication were also significantly upregulated, consistent with the rapid cell proliferation at this stage observed by flow cytometry (Figure 2), and further suggesting a high metabolic rate.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq and flow cytometry data.

claim: Cystic cells showed significant downregulation of genes associated with myosin transport, translation, DNA replication and metabolic activities compared to filopodial and aggregative cells.
source: When compared to filopodial and aggregative cells, cystic cells showed significant downregulation of genes associated with myosin transport, translation, DNA replication and metabolic activities (especially mitochondrial energy production).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq and GO enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes involved in vesicle transport and autophagy were significantly upregulated in the cystic stage.
source: However, genes involved in vesicle transport and autophagy were significantly upregulated at this stage (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq and GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The gene expression differences in cystic cells may reflect recycling of intracellular components triggered by starvation or other adverse conditions.
source: These differences may reflect recycling of intracellular components triggered by starvation or other adverse conditions, as has been observed under conditions of adaptive cell survival in other eukaryotes (Kiel, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to similar processes in other organisms.

claim: Protein domains involved in the ubiquitin pathway were significantly upregulated in cystic cells.
source: Protein domains involved in the ubiquitin pathway (e.g., UQ_con, zf-RING2 and Cullin domains) and in synaptic cell–cell communication, such as SNARE, synaptobrevin and syntaxin, as well specific transcription factor families (e.g., bHLH transcription factors), were also significantly upregulated in the cystic cells (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by Pfam domain enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The integrin adhesome and associated tyrosine kinase signalling genes likely play an important role in the formation of C. owczarzaki aggregates.
source: These observations strongly suggest that the integrin adhesome and the likely associated tyrosine kinase signalling genes play an important role in the formation of the C. owzarzaki aggregates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed upregulation of these genes during aggregation.

claim: Genes involved in mitosis and in the tubulin cytoskeleton were upregulated at the aggregative stage.
source: Furthermore, we also observed upregulation of genes involved in mitosis and in the tubulin cytoskeleton (e.g., kinesins) at the aggregative stage (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq and GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: A molecular repertoire associated with animal multicellularity could function either in aggregative or in clonal multicellularity and in different phylogenetic contexts.
source: These results indicate that a molecular repertoire associated with animal multicellularity, could function either in aggregative or in clonal multicellularity and in different phylogenetic contexts, in line with previous hypotheses (Newman, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed gene expression patterns, supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Of 25,677 introns with sufficient RNA-Seq read coverage across the three life cycle stages, 2986 (11.6%) showed ≥20% PSI in at least one stage.
source: Of 25,677 introns with sufficient RNA-Seq read coverage across the three life cycle stages, 2986 (11.6%) showed ≥20% PSI (Percent Spliced In, percent of transcripts from a given gene in which the intron sequence is present) in at least one stage, and approximately a third of genes had at least one such intron retention event.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of intron retention.

claim: 797 retained introns (in 441 genes) display differential PSI values of 25% or more in the filopodial stage compared to the other stages.
source: In particular, 797 retained introns (in 441 genes) and 259 retained introns (in 232 genes) display differential PSI (dPSI) values of 25% or more in the filopodial and cystic stages compared to the other stages, respectively (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: 259 retained introns (in 232 genes) display differential PSI values of 25% or more in the cystic stage compared to the other stages.
source: In particular, 797 retained introns (in 441 genes) and 259 retained introns (in 232 genes) display differential PSI (dPSI) values of 25% or more in the filopodial and cystic stages compared to the other stages, respectively (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: No retained introns were found to be differentially spliced at the aggregative stage.
source: In contrast, no retained introns were found to be differentially spliced at the aggregative stage.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of intron retention.

claim: Most (12 out of 15, 80%) of the analyzed cases of differentially retained introns were validated by RT-PCR.
source: Most (12 out of 15, 80%) of the analyzed cases of differentially retained introns were validated by RT-PCR (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR validation experiments shown in Figure 9C.

claim: GO enrichment analysis for the two sets of differentially retained introns showed distinct gene function enrichment.
source: GO enrichment analysis for the two sets of differentially retained introns showed distinct gene function enrichment (e.g., protein kinase activity and intracellular targeting in the filopodial stage, and histone modification and myosin complex in the cystic stage) (Figure 6), implying that regulated intron retention plays different roles at these stages.
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Most if not all differentially retained introns act by reducing the levels of spliced mRNAs exported from the nucleus and translated into protein.
source: A low fraction of read-through introns (with length-multiples of three and no in-frame stop codons) were found among the two sets of differentially retained introns, suggesting that most if not all of these retained introns act by reducing the levels of spliced mRNAs exported from the nucleus and translated into protein, as has been observed previously for regulated retained introns in metazoan species (Yap et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of retained intron sequences, supported by citation to similar mechanisms in metazoans.

claim: Multiple introns belonging to a gene can be retained in a stage-specific manner in C. owczarzaki.
source: Moreover, we observe that multiple introns belonging to a gene can be retained in a stage-specific manner. For instance, >73% and >29% of multi-intronic genes with one differentially retained intron had at least one additional differentially retained intron at the filopodial or cystic-specific stages, respectively, and 22% and 5% of genes at these stages showed evidence of high retention for all introns in the same genes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of intron retention patterns.

claim: Multiple intron retention events often occur in a combinatorial manner in C. owczarzaki.
source: Furthermore, RT-PCR analyses and mate information from paired-end read analyses suggested that multiple intron retention events often occur in a combinatorial manner (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), thereby increasing the potential impact of intron retentions on mRNA regulation.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and paired-end read analysis.

claim: Filopodial-specific differentially retained introns have a similar length distribution to constitutive introns.
source: While filopodial-specific differentially retained introns have a similar length distribution to constitutive (PSI less than 2% across all stages) introns, cystic stage-specific introns were significantly longer (p=1.7e−14 Wilcoxon rank sum test) (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of intron lengths shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Cystic stage-specific retained introns were significantly longer than constitutive introns.
source: While filopodial-specific differentially retained introns have a similar length distribution to constitutive (PSI less than 2% across all stages) introns, cystic stage-specific introns were significantly longer (p=1.7e−14 Wilcoxon rank sum test) (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of intron lengths shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The average level of intron retention increased steadily with intron length only in the cystic stage.
source: In line with this observation, the average level of intron retention increased steadily with intron length only in the cystic stage (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Cystic stage-specific retained introns harbored significantly weaker canonical 5´ and 3´ splice site signals than other intron sets.
source: Furthermore, cystic stage-specific retained introns harbored significantly weaker canonical 5´ and 3´ splice site signals than other intron sets (p<0.0013 Wilcoxon rank sum test for all comparisons).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of splice site sequences.

claim: Differential intron retention in the cystic stage may be associated with suboptimal introns that are more efficiently spliced in the other cell stages.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that differential intron retention in the cystic stage may be associated with suboptimal introns (i.e., long and with weak splice sites) that are more efficiently spliced in the other cell stages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of intron length and splice site strength.

claim: Filopodial-specific differentially retained introns show enrichment of a long T/G-rich motif that highly resembles a consensus binding site for Elav-like protein in mammals.
source: In the case of the filopodial-specific differentially retained introns, analyses of sequence motif enrichment with MEME show enrichment of a long T/G-rich motif that highly resembles a recently identified consensus binding site for Elav-like protein in mammals (Ince-Dunn et al., 2012) (Figure 10).
evidence: This is supported by MEME analysis and comparison to known binding sites, shown in Figure 10.

claim: The single ortholog for Elav-like protein in C. owczarzaki shows a highly-regulated expression pattern, with lowest expression in the filopodial stage.
source: Interestingly, the single ortholog for this gene in C. owczarzaki shows a highly-regulated expression pattern, with lowest expression in the filopodial stage (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq expression data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Elav-like protein may negatively regulate filopodial-specific intron retention of some introns.
source: Therefore, it is tempting to speculate that Elav-like protein may negatively regulate filopodial-specific intron retention of some introns.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the motif enrichment and expression pattern.

claim: 191 cassette exons with PSIs <95% in at least one life cycle stage were identified in C. owczarzaki.
source: Next, we investigated differential exon splicing and identified 191 cassette exons with PSIs <95% in at least one life cycle stage, 39 of which display PSIs <85%.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of exon skipping.

claim: 29 cassette exons showed a ≥15% PSI difference in pairwise comparisons between the cell stages, with lower PSIs typically associated with the filopodial stage.
source: 29 of these exons showed a ≥15% PSI difference in pairwise comparisons between the cell stages, with lower PSIs typically associated with the filopodial stage (Supplementary file 1); RT-PCR assays confirmed skipping for 7 out of 8 tested cases (Figure 11A, and Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis and RT-PCR validation shown in Figure 11A.

claim: Most (∼60%) of the differentially-regulated exons in C. owczarzaki maintain an open reading frame when skipped.
source: Most (∼60%) of these exons maintain an open reading frame when skipped.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of exon sequences.

claim: Two thirds of the differently regulated exons in C. owczarzaki overlap annotated domains.
source: In contrast to previous reports demonstrating that differentially-regulated exons are significantly under represented in modular, folded domains in metazoans (Romero et al., 2006; Ellis et al., 2012), two thirds of the differently regulated exons in C. owczarzaki overlap annotated domains (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by domain annotation analysis, contrasting with cited metazoan studies.

claim: Genes with differential exon skipping in C. owczarzaki are statistically significantly enriched in protein kinase activity.
source: Furthermore, genes with differential exon skipping are statistically significantly enriched in protein kinase activity, impacting both tyrosine and serine/threonine kinases (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 11B.

claim: Coordinated exon skipping plays a role in the modulation of cell signaling in C. owczarzaki.
source: This observation strongly suggests a role for coordinated exon skipping in the modulation of cell signaling in C. owczarzaki.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of protein kinase genes among those with differential exon skipping.

claim: The regulated exon network linked to signaling in C. owczarzaki represents the first example of such a network in a unicellular organism.
source: To our knowledge, this represents the first example of a regulated exon network linked to a specific biological function in a unicellular organism.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed data and review of literature.

claim: The observation of an aggregative multicellular stage in C. owczarzaki represents the first example of such cellular behavior in a close unicellular relative of metazoans.
source: In particular, the observation of an aggregative multicellular stage in C. owczarzaki represents the first example of such cellular behavior in a close unicellular relative of metazoans.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and review of literature.

claim: The current evolutionary framework on the opisthokonts discards the possibility that C. owczarzaki derives from a more complex multicellular lineage.
source: We note that the current evolutionary framework on the opisthokonts, based on phylogenomic analyses (Steenkamp et al., 2006; Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008; Shalchian-Tabrizi et al., 2008; Torruella et al., 2012; Paps et al., 2013), discards the possibility that C. owczarzaki (or choanoflagellates) derives from a more complex multicellular lineage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to phylogenomic studies.

claim: The sister-group of opisthokonts is the unicellular biflagellates Apusozoa.
source: The sister-group of opisthokonts is the unicellular biflagellates Apusozoa, and complex multicellularity has not yet been observed in any of the non-metazoan holozoan lineages.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic relationships established in the literature.

claim: Complex multicellularity has not yet been observed in any of the non-metazoan holozoan lineages.
source: The sister-group of opisthokonts is the unicellular biflagellates Apusozoa, and complex multicellularity has not yet been observed in any of the non-metazoan holozoan lineages.
evidence: This is based on review of the literature on holozoan diversity.

claim: The complex, metazoan-like genetic 'toolkit' of C. owczarzaki is dynamically deployed during its highly-regulated life cycle.
source: Furthermore, we show that the complex, metazoan-like genetic 'toolkit' of C. owczarzaki (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2010, 2011; Suga et al., 2012) is dynamically deployed during its highly-regulated life cycle, with upregulation of integrin adhesome and signalling genes linked to multicellularity in metazoans during the aggregative stage.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data showing stage-specific gene expression patterns.

claim: Extensive differential alternative splicing between the C. owczarzaki life cycle stages likely contributes to the dynamic gene regulation observed in this species.
source: Extensive differential AS between the C. owczarzaki life cycle stages likely further contributes to the dynamic gene regulation observed in this species, with differential intron retention likely acting as an important mechanism in the control of transcript levels between life cycle stages, probably through triggering non-sense mediated decay (NMD).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed alternative splicing patterns.

claim: Differential intron retention likely acts as an important mechanism in the control of transcript levels between life cycle stages in C. owczarzaki, probably through triggering non-sense mediated decay (NMD).
source: Extensive differential AS between the C. owczarzaki life cycle stages likely further contributes to the dynamic gene regulation observed in this species, with differential intron retention likely acting as an important mechanism in the control of transcript levels between life cycle stages, probably through triggering non-sense mediated decay (NMD).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed intron retention patterns and known mechanisms in other organisms.

claim: The emergence of an exon network that functions in conjunction with differentially-regulated intron retention may have provided a degree of proteomic and regulatory complexity that was key in the evolution of cell type complexity in metazoans.
